newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan ethnic party accuses army of rigging.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan ethnic party accuses army of rigging.

text.p: Pakistan's ethnic Mohajir National Movement (MQM) accused the army on Monday of involvement in what it called election rigging in Karachi and other towns in the southern province of Sindh.

"We hold the army directly responsible for the blatant rigging and violence against our supporters and polling agents," Senator Ishtiaq Azhar, chief of the MQM's co-ordination committee, told reporters in Karachi.

Azhar said two MQM supporters, one of them a polling agent and brother of an MQM candidate, were killed and three wounded, while several MQM polling agents were kidnapped or beaten up as polling stations were "literally occupied by our opponents".
He said the breakaway MQM-Haqiqi faction had carried out these activities in front of troops guarding polling stations.
"These incidents could not have taken place without the involvement of the army," Azhar said.
About 250,000 members of the armed forces were deployed across Pakistan to provide security during nine hours of voting for national and provincial assemblies.
"A number of our polling agents are still missing," he said, adding that troops had arrested an MQM candidate from the town of Mirpukhas on unspecified charges and he was still detained.
"I think these activities were part of a pre-determined plan to show that MQM has lost its vote-bank and is no longer as popular as it used to be a few years back," he said.
Azhar listed several irregularities in the voting, similar to those identified by a spokesman of Benazir Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party at a news conference earlier.
"Voting was deliberately delayed to show a low turnout and polling stations were changed during vote-casting confusing a large number of voters," Azhar said.

The MQM and the breakaway MQM-Haqiqi faction traded charges of harassment through the day. MQM-Haqiqi eventually said it was boycotting the last hour of polling. The faction has never won an election and had not been expected to gain any seats.
Hundreds of people have died in feuding between MQM factions in the past four years. The MQM speaks for Urdu-speakers who migrated to Pakistan from India in 1947 and their descendants.
The army and MQM have been at odds since June 1992 when troops launched a major security sweep in the cities of Sindh.
About 500 people were killed in ethnic, sectarian and political violence in Karachi last year, compared to more than 2,000 in 1995 and about 800 in 1994.
Monday's elections followed President Farooq Leghari's removal of former prime minister Benazir Bhutto on November 5.
Leghari accused her government of corruption, nepotism and extra-judicial killings in Karachi and the Supreme Court ruled last week that the president's action had been justified.
In other election day unrest, five people were killed when two groups clashed over a land dispute near a polling station in Gujranwala in the central province of Punjab, police said.
